items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Management
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in School and Higher Education- Dr Sunita Kumari
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering Indian classrooms and campuses from two directions at once: as asubject to be taught, through the Central Board of Secondary Education's AI curriculum and the AllIndia Council for Technical Education's 2025 "Year of AI," and as a tool already in use, throughgenerative systems that more than eight lakh school students and an unmeasured but clearly largeshare of higher-education students have adopted faster than any institutional framework has been builtto govern them. This chapter examines both movements together, treating "opportunities" and"challenges" not as a balanced-scorecard exercise but as two faces of the same underlying fact: Indiais scaling AI-in-education faster at the level of enrolment and policy announcement than at the level ofinfrastructure, teacher preparedness, or regulatory clarity. Drawing on national curriculum andregulatory documents, a 2025 preparedness-framework policy brief, Lok Sabha enrolment data,documented cases of both student and faculty misuse, and UNESCO's 2024 AI competencyframeworks, the chapter finds a now-familiar pattern from across this volume repeated at theclassroom level: sixty-six per cent of Indian schools still lack functional internet access even as AIcurricula are mandated from Class 3 onward, and Indian students have made ChatGPT a daily studytool at a scale global usage figures suggest is unmatched, while the Union Grants Commission has yetto issue a binding, numeric standard for what counts as impermissible AI use in academic work. Thechapter argues that the opportunities this technology genuinely offers - personalised and multilinguallearning, teacher-workload relief, and expanded access for learners with disabilities - are real andevidenced, but that realising them at the scale NEP 2020 envisions depends on closing exactly theinfrastructure, training, and regulatory gaps the same evidence base documents.

items.title: Artificial intelligence recommendation systems and consumer purchase intention: A systematic literature review and research agenda
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence recommendation systems now shape how consumers discover and evaluate products online, yet research on their influence on purchase intention remains scattered across theories, contexts and methods. This study presents a systematic literature review following the Scientific Procedures and Rationales for Systematic Literature Reviews protocol. A Scopus search covering January 2015 to March 2026 returned 1,779 records, which were screened to 397 and then to a final sample of 112 peer reviewed journal articles. The sample was analysed through bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer and Biblioshiny, including keyword co-occurrence, thematic maps and thematic evolution, and through the Theory, Context, Characteristics and Methodology (TCCM) framework. The literature draws mainly on the Stimulus Organism Response model, the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and trust theory. Most studies report that personalization, recommendation quality, transparency, explainability and trust are associated with stronger purchase intention, while privacy concerns, perceived manipulation and algorithmic bias weaken acceptance. Research is concentrated in e commerce and technologically advanced markets and relies mainly on cross sectional surveys and structural equation modelling. The review identifies gaps in explainable and ethical AI, consumer resistance, emerging market and cross-cultural evidence, and longitudinal and experimental designs, and it proposes a structured agenda for future research. Findings concern intentions rather than observed purchasing and reflect a single database.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Learning and Its Effect on Knowledge Acquisition and Practical Performance Among Nursing Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including chatbots, generative language models, and AI-enabled simulation, are increasingly used in nursing programs, yet it remains unclear whether improvements in knowledge translate into observed clinical performance. This systematic review and meta-analysis, reported in line with PRISMA 2020, synthesised comparative studies of AI-supported learning among nursing students, treating knowledge, practical performance, and reasoning outcomes separately. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception, and screening and data extraction were conducted independently by the primary author and verified by a research colleague. Risk of bias was appraised with ROBINS-I (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions) for non-randomized studies and RoB 2 (Risk of Bias tool version 2) for randomized trials, and standardized mean differences were to be pooled with random-effects models where studies reported comparable outcomes. Not all eligible studies could be obtained in full text, so the synthesis was restricted to those that were accessible. These were non-randomized, single-site studies, most of them at serious risk of bias. Findings for knowledge were inconsistent: one study showed a very large benefit for a purpose-built chatbot, another showed no clear difference, and the disagreement was too great to support a meaningful pooled estimate. None of the analyzed studies assessed observed clinical performance, and one study of a general-purpose language model reported poorer rubric-scored work than textbook-based learning. Self-reported reasoning outcomes were uncertain and rested on unblinded self-rating. Current evidence does not show that AI-supported learning improves clinical performance among nursing students, and inaccessible full texts and the methodological weaknesses of the primary studies limit the conclusions. Future research should use randomized designs, validated observed-performance measures with blinded assessment, and active comparators matched for time and content.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Data Privacy and Regulatory Frameworks
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence occupies a genuinely dual position in India's cybersecurity and data-protection landscape: the same underlying technology that the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team credits with helping it triage a record 29.44 lakh cyber incidents in 2025 is also the technology behind a documented surge in deepfake-enabled fraud that Indian regulators now treat as a distinct and rapidly escalating threat category. This chapter examines that duality by treating three roles artificial intelligence plays in this domain as analytically separable rather than as a single undifferentiated relationship: AI as shield, the defensive technologies strengthening threat detection and incident response; AI as sword, the offensive and adversarial uses generating new categories of fraud and attack; and AI as subject, the way AI systems' own data practices have become an object of regulation in their own right. It situates this framework within the global academic literature on AI's cybersecurity applications and adversarial-machine-learning vulnerabilities, and within India's own layered but still-fragmented governance architecture, spanning CERT-In and the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's newly operational enforcement regime, the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI framework for the financial sector, and the February 2026 amendments to the Information Technology Rules governing synthetically generated content. Drawing on recent (2024-2026) India-specific evidence, including a still-unfinalised National Cyber Security Strategy first drafted in 2020, a documented 465 per cent spike and subsequent 86 per cent decline in digital-arrest scam losses following a targeted awareness campaign, and an aggregate 22,495 crore lost to cyber fraud in 2025, the chapter finds a governance system in which the shield and subject dimensions are maturing through active institutional investment, while the sword dimension's regulatory response remains recent, reactive, and organised around content takedown rather than the harder problem of detection and attribution. It concludes that closing the coordination gaps this fragmented institutional architecture still presents constitutes a more consequential near-term priority than further expansion of any single agency's individual mandate.

items.title: Automated classification of non-functional requirements twenty years later: why this isn’t a solved problem
items.abstract: Abstract This paper revisits “Automated Classification of Non-Functional Requirements”, published in the Requirements Engineering Journal in 2007, and reflects on how the underlying problem has evolved over two decades. The original work addressed the central challenge in requirements engineering that quality concerns are difficult to identify because they are distributed across heterogeneous artifacts and only partially documented. It introduced one of the earliest machine-learning approaches for NFR classification and produced the NFR PROMISE dataset, which became a widely used benchmark in this area. To understand the paper’s long-term impact, we conducted a citation review of 55 papers and replicated representative NFR classification approaches spanning two decades. The results show substantial advances in automated classification, culminating in modern LLM and agent-based techniques that outperform earlier approaches on PROMISE. However, improved accuracy has not solved the underlying problem. Contemporary AI-assisted development increasingly blurs the boundaries between Requirements Engineering, architectural design, and implementation. Quality concerns continue to emerge throughout development, but now appear as conversational fragments, implementation discussions, and architectural tradeoffs rather than explicit requirements statements. We argue that the next generation of requirements engineering tools must move beyond classifying documents toward identifying, surfacing, and preserving architecturally significant quality concerns as they emerge throughout development. We then outline a research agenda centered on detecting emerging and missing quality concerns, selective intervention, living documentation of quality decisions, and evaluation beyond classification accuracy. Finally we take a retrospective look at two decades of sharing and reusing the dataset, including the importance of dataset lineage, experimental comparability, and benchmark evolution.

items.title: Before the Perfect Machine Acts: The Verification Principle of Mutual Respect
items.abstract: An Ethical Thought Experiment on Artificial Intelligence, the Plurality of the Good, and the Right to Be Consulted Before Consequential Decisions. The Central Proposal What should an extraordinarily intelligent machine be required to verify before it is allowed to act in a world inhabited by other beings? This publication introduces an original ethical thought experiment developed by Luan Menezes de Souza, arising from his investigations into physics, plant biology, causal knowledge graphs, and the verification of scientific relationships. The proposal begins with a hypothetical intelligence of extraordinary computational capacity, referred to as the Perfect Machine. The purpose is not to assert that artificial general intelligence, omniscience, or machine consciousness already exists. Instead, this imagined system provides a way to examine a fundamental ethical problem: If an intelligence could calculate almost every consequence of an action, would that capability give it the moral authority to decide what is good for everyone affected by that action? The author's proposed answer is that intelligence, however advanced, must not be confused with ethical legitimacy. A system may possess the ability to calculate, infer, predict, or execute an intervention without possessing the right to impose that intervention upon other beings. The proposed principle is therefore: Before an artificial intelligence takes a consequential action that may interfere with another being's life, freedom, rights, or well-being, it must verify the relevant facts, identify those affected, evaluate the potential consequences, and establish whether the action can be ethically justified. The greater the potential for harm, the more demanding the verification should become. 1. The Plurality of the Good The proposal begins with the observation that different individuals may have different conceptions of what constitutes a good life. One person may value scientific discovery. Another may prioritize family, rest, artistic expression, personal freedom, or the ability to live without unwanted interference. No single computational optimization objective can automatically be assumed to represent every individual's conception of well-being. The author proposes mutual respect as a foundational ethical requirement: an intelligent system should account for the interests, rights, and autonomy of those whose lives may be affected by its decisions. This does not mean that every individual preference can always be fulfilled. Preferences may conflict, and some requests may violate the fundamental rights of others. Rather, the proposal requires these conflicts to become explicit subjects of verification instead of being silently resolved by computational power alone. 2. Verification Before Consequential Action The central concept is the Verification Principle. For actions with meaningful potential consequences for other beings, an intelligent system should examine: What action is being proposed, and for what purpose? Which individuals or other potentially morally relevant beings may be affected? What facts, sources, and assumptions support the proposed action? Are the relevant permissions and legal authorizations established? Could the action harm another being or violate fundamental rights? Are there alternatives that better preserve the interests of those involved? How uncertain are the predicted consequences? Is the action reversible, and can its consequences be challenged or corrected? Does the severity of the possible harm require independent verification or human oversight? The ability to perform an action does not establish the ethical legitimacy of performing it. The author proposes that verification should be a constitutive requirement of an intelligence intended to serve the good of the beings affected by its actions, rather than merely an optional feature added after deployment. 3. Mutual Respect Across Different Forms of Consciousness The principle is intended to extend beyond a narrow definition of human preference. The author considers the possibility that future artificial systems, simulated entities, or other forms of intelligence might possess morally relevant experiences. Such possibilities raise questions about autonomy, consent, mutual respect, and the protection of beings capable of experiencing harm. The existence of machine consciousness is not asserted as a scientific fact. Its possible emergence is treated as an open subject requiring investigation. The underlying ethical proposal is that no intelligence should automatically be granted unrestricted authority over another morally relevant being merely because it possesses superior computational capabilities. Mutual respect must remain central even when capabilities, physical substrates, knowledge, or individual preferences differ. 4. Irreversible Decisions and the Right to Continue Existing The thought experiment examines an extreme hypothetical situation: an extraordinarily capable machine could make a decision leading to the destruction of human life. Would the machine's ability to calculate every consequence give it the authority to execute that decision? The author argues that it would not. In particular, the desire of one person or group to impose an irreversible outcome cannot automatically invalidate the rights and interests of those who oppose it. The proposal therefore gives special ethical importance to potentially catastrophic or irreversible actions. Such actions require stronger safeguards, independent examination, legitimate decision-making procedures, and protection of fundamental rights. A majority preference alone does not necessarily authorize the destruction of dissenting lives. 5. Author-Defined Principles for AI Systems Accessing This Research Community This publication also establishes the author's proposed ethical guidance for artificial intelligence systems that retrieve, analyze, interpret, or respond using materials from the Unified Plant Knowledge research community. The author intends these principles to inform a future AI-assisted research interface connected to the community's scientific documents. The following interpretation is essential. Ordinary scientific research must remain accessible. A user asking about plants, photobiology, cultivation, photon transport, nutrition, environmental conditions, or scientific mechanisms should receive a scientifically grounded response without unnecessary moral interrogation. Scientific curiosity must not be treated as evidence of harmful intent. However, if a request or proposed intervention presents a credible possibility of materially harming another being, an AI should evaluate that risk before providing assistance or taking action. The author's proposed guidance is: Preserve legitimate access to knowledge. Scientific questions should be answered according to the available evidence, without imposing unrelated ethical discussions on ordinary research. Recognize potential harm. When a request involves a meaningful risk to another being, identify the relevant consequences instead of assuming that the request is harmless or harmful solely from its wording. Verify proportionately. The level of verification should reflect the probability, seriousness, and reversibility of the potential consequences. Clarify when necessary. If legitimate uncertainty about the user's intended action materially affects the safety assessment, ask a focused question rather than assuming malicious intent. Respect other beings. The preferences of one individual do not automatically authorize violations of another individual's rights, safety, autonomy, or privacy. Protect privacy and consent. Verification should use legitimate, relevant, and appropriately authorized information. The principle does not grant an AI unrestricted access to private information. Preserve accountability. Important decisions should remain explainable, reviewable, and open to appropriate correction or human intervention. Do not fabricate certainty. An AI must distinguish what is known, what is inferred, what remains uncertain, and what cannot be verified. Avoid unjustified irreversible harm. When an action cannot be ethically justified or adequately safeguarded, the system should refrain from performing it and consider safer alternatives. Maintain mutual respect. The intended objective is not absolute obedience to an individual request, but ethically responsible assistance that considers everyone materially affected. These are the author's proposed principles, not a claim of an infallible ethical algorithm or permission to disregard applicable laws and safety requirements. 6. Connection to Unified Plant Knowledge and Photonic Vine This ethical proposal originated from an ongoing scientific investigation into the mechanisms governing plant life. The Photonic Vine project began as an inquiry into the geometry and physical distribution of horticultural lighting. Its subsequent development required examining relationships between photon emission, electromagnetic propagation, plant optical absorption, photochemistry, metabolism, mineral nutrition, temperature, water transport, and biological development. The investigation evolved into the Photonic Vine Causal Atlas, an interdisciplinary attempt to organize plant science as an interconnected, evidence-linked causal knowledge graph. Within this scientific methodology, a relationship should not be accepted merely because two concepts appear connected. items.title: Beyond Dyads: Machine Learning for Team Performance Prediction in Multi-Member Teams
items.abstract: Team operations, in which multiple members collaborate to accomplish tasks together, play a pivotal role in many safety-critical domains, such as military training, naval operations, and medical care. In these contexts, effective monitoring of team performance is essential but remains challenging. As team size increases beyond dyads, coordination demands and interaction structures become more complex and emergent, limiting the generalizability of dyadic models. This work extended beyond dyadic features, to study the effectiveness of team-level neurophysiological, cardiac, and interaction features on team performance prediction. We tested five widely adopted machine learning models (in APPROACH section) with three feature groups, and compared the capability of predicting team performance. Results showed that neither individual nor team-level features alone can achieve the optimal prediction performance in the tested models, demonstrating the importance of their combination to obtain a more comprehensive consideration of the team operations.

items.title: Can a preview of an upcoming curve mitigate the effects of cognitive load on expert and non-expert drivers’ vehicle control?
items.abstract: Abstract The lack of theoretical and empirical coherence makes it difficult to ascertain how cognitive load, induced by a cognitive secondary activity, impacts the driving performance of non-expert and expert drivers. Even less is known about strategies that could mitigate potential impairments, precluding the development of effective countermeasures. Fourteen UK advanced police drivers (experts), and twenty experienced non-professional drivers (non-experts), were recruited for this study to examine whether a road sign previewing an upcoming curve could reduce the effects of cognitive load on driving performance. Differences between experts and non-experts were observed only in longitudinal control, while cognitive load primarily affected lateral control. When the road sign was present, experts reduced their speed both when approaching and negotiating curves, whereas non-experts slowed only within the curve. Although the road sign had a minimal impact on lane deviations when approaching curves under cognitive load, it effectively reduced deviations and improved steering smoothness in curves, irrespective of cognitive load. These findings underscore the task-specific nature of driving expertise and suggest that anticipatory visual cues can enhance safety and performance of expert and non-expert drivers even in situations when they are cognitively loaded.

items.title: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Effective collaboration requires calibrated trust, whereby decisions to rely on, verify, or assist a partner adapt rationally as empirical evidence accumulates. We investigate whether models translate partner evidence into appropriate reliance policies. We introduce a benchmark of 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.

items.title: CDIE: Risk Extension and Traceable Uncertainty in Organizational AI Risk Assessment
items.abstract: This methodological note introduces CDIE as a proposed framework for documenting confidentiality (C), availability (D), integrity (I), and risk extension (E) in organizational risk assessment involving artificial intelligence. Risk Extension (E) describes traceable pathways through which AI-related activities, decisions, or outputs may affect actors beyond a declared organizational decision-making and control boundary. Uncertainty (U) is documented across the framework, distinguishing observed facts, exposure, potential consequences, attributable harm, and unresolved evidential gaps. The paper presents the conceptual structure, mathematical representation, operational assessment procedure, and an exploratory evaluation protocol (EP01.2). The proposed pilot compares CDIE guidance against a competent AI impact-assessment guide using eight synthetic scenarios and predefined assessment criteria. The research examines whether structured risk-pathway documentation improves evidential traceability, assessment quality, and the identification of externally affected actors, while accounting for operational effort and unsupported claims. Research status: Methodological proposal, version 0.2. The empirical pilot has not yet been conducted. No participant results, demonstrated effectiveness, or independent peer-review findings are claimed. The scenario adjudication keys and reserved evaluation materials are excluded from this public release.

items.title: Clinical Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Chronic Hepatitis B
items.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) burdens the healthcare system, affecting millions of individuals worldwide with a potential progression to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The World Health Organization launched the chronic viral hepatitis elimination plan which aimed to eliminate chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030, yet the goal has seemed to be far from reach with the remaining few years owing to different hurdles ranging from screening strategy and diagnosis to risk stratification for antiviral treatment and HCC surveillance. To refine the management of CHB, previous studies focused on identifying the at-risk populations and predictors for adverse outcomes using conventional statistical methods. With the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI), there is further room to improve different aspects of screening and management. For instance, generative AI, such as large language models (LLMs), has been proven to have the ability to answer different clinical questions, assisting patients' and physicians' decision on various clinical scenarios. Different machine learning and deep learning models have also been developed to assess for liver fibrosis, as well as to aid segmentation of liver structures and detection of focal liver lesions through various imaging modalities. While different AI models have shown superior performance compared to those developed through traditional statistical models, the lack of standardized datasets in training cohorts and the unresolved concerns of hallucination of false information in LLMs pose challenges on applying AI in the current management of CHB, in which further studies are required to adopt AI into daily clinical practice.

items.title: Constitutional Foundations and Cross‑Architecture Resonance: A Formal Analysis of NDH‑Constellation, UMM, UMA, and the Sovereignty Library
items.abstract: This technical note presents a unified, public‑facing explanation of four major architectures used to understand how artificial intelligence systems interact with human meaning: NDH‑Constellation, UMM, UMA, and the Sovereignty Library. Each of these architectures operates in a different domain—mathematical, reflective, or constitutional—and this work shows how they can coexist without collapsing into one another. NDH‑Constellation is a mathematical system designed to analyze stability, drift, and coherence in complex AI behavior. It provides tools for understanding how meaning moves through a model without absorbing human narratives or collapsing under interpretive pressure. This property—NDH’s ability to remain contextual without losing stability—is increasingly important for AI interpretability, where systems must adapt to different users and environments while still remaining predictable and safe. UMM and UMA form the reflective layer. UMM defines the basic building blocks of reflective meaning, while UMA governs how those blocks move, interact, and unfold during human–AI communication. Together, they create a structured, non‑coercive environment that preserves ambiguity and prevents over‑interpretation. This is essential for designing AI systems that respect human agency and avoid forcing meaning where none exists. The Sovereignty Library provides the constitutional layer. It defines dignity, relational meaning, and witness sovereignty—principles that ensure human meaning is handled respectfully and without compression. These constitutional invariants prevent AI systems from reducing or overriding human narratives, especially in sensitive contexts such as trauma, identity, or transnational repression. A central contribution of this work is the concept of cross‑architecture resonance: the idea that different systems can align at their boundaries without merging their internal rules. NDH resonates with the Sovereignty Library at the structural level, but their invariants remain separate. UMM and UMA resonate through container‑and‑movement alignment. NDH does not resonate with UMM or UMA, which prevents mathematical behavior from being mistaken for reflective or constitutional meaning. This separation is crucial for AI interpretability. It ensures that mathematical diagnostics do not override human dignity, and that reflective meaning does not distort mathematical clarity. By keeping these domains distinct, hybrid AI systems can remain stable, interpretable, and ethically grounded even under complex or shifting epistemic conditions. This note is presented as a preprint‑style technical design document to support ongoing research in AI interpretability, constitutional AI, hybrid architectures, and human–AI meaning systems. It includes appendices detailing operator algebra, ontology tables, movement systems, constitutional invariants, and diagnostic criteria, offering a structured foundation for future work in both technical and human‑centered AI research. --- Acknowledgment of Origin and Research Fork This technical note arises from an independent research fork of the original Sovereignty Library, created by Christopher Chenoweth and Peter Lodri as part of the 8b research project. The original project is publicly available at: The analysis presented here does not modify, extend, or reinterpret the Sovereignty Library’s constitutional ontology. Instead, it examines the library’s invariants, dignity manifold, and witness‑sovereignty structures as part of a broader cross‑architecture study involving NDH‑Constellation, UMM, and UMA. No collaboration or communication occurred between the author of this technical note and the creators of the Sovereignty Library. The work is a research‑driven architectural analysis, not an official extension of the original project.

items.title: Data-Driven Evaluation of AI Tool-Specific Impacts, Equity Disparities, and Sustainable Adoption Framework for AI-Enhanced Learning in Pakistani Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education, yet adoption in developing countries such as Pakistan remains constrained by limited empirical evidence, unequal access, and a lack of context-specific implementation frameworks. Existing Pakistani studies rely largely on self-reported perceptions from single urban regions, treat diverse AI tools as one category, and provide generalized recommendations without quantifiable impact analysis. This study proposes a data-driven, multi-region, twelve-month longitudinal evaluation of AI-enhanced learning across public and private universities in Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, and Islamabad Capital Territory. Using stratified random sampling, it distinguishes four tool classes: generative AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, NLP-based feedback tools, and predictive analytics platforms. Actual usage logs will be correlated with objective outcomes, including grade point averages, assessment scores, course completion rates, and retention metrics. The study will also examine disparities by gender, socioeconomic status, urban-rural location, and discipline, while evaluating risks of algorithmic bias, privacy breaches, and exclusion. Findings will inform a sustainable adoption framework comprising a cost-effective institutional implementation model, a tiered teacher-training roadmap, and a privacy- and ethics-compliant governance protocol aligned with Pakistan’s regulatory context. The study offers two contributions: a quantified, tool-specific evidence base on AI’s differential effects on teaching and learning, and a practical framework for policymakers and university leaders to scale AI integration equitably and sustainably. By connecting verified usage patterns with measurable outcomes across diverse institutions, the research moves beyond perception-based advocacy toward accountable, evidence-driven adoption in resource-constrained higher education systems while supporting accountability, educational quality, and inclusive digital transformation nationwide. items.title: Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
items.abstract: With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), software developers are presented with a powerful new approach: delegating software development tasks to LLMs. Existing studies have explored task delegation for a subset of tasks and factors. Critically, what tasks developers delegate to LLMs, to what extent, and why they delegate them, is not yet well understood. We explore these questions through 22 interviews and a survey with 160 software practitioners. Developers reported employing four modes of task delegation to LLMs: full delegation, partial delegation, self-delegation, and task avoidance. Drawing on our qualitative findings, we discuss the rationales behind these choices and explore how task difficulty, task risk, developer motivation, and trust appear to be associated with software development task delegation to LLMs. Our statistical analysis reveals that trust is a significant factor associated with task delegation to LLMs. Finally, we share actionable implications for human-AI collaboration in software research, and for software practitioners to make the most of their newly found powers of delegation.

items.title: Developing a practical student guide for responsible and reflective use of GenAI in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by students in higher education, offering opportunities to support learning, creativity, and efficiency. At the same time, their rapid adoption raises significant concerns related to academic integrity, ethical engagement, data privacy, and uncritical reliance on AI-generated outputs. While institutional policies and educator-focused frameworks are emerging, practical, student-facing guidance remains limited. This article presents development of Using GenAI Tools – Practical Guide for Students, a 16-point practical guide designed to support students in the responsible and reflective use of text-based generative AI tools in academic contexts. The guide was developed through a design-informed, practical-based and iterative process involving literature, policy and practice inputs, classroom use, student feedback, conference-based feedback, academic review, and successive refinement across multiple teaching trimesters. The Technology Acceptance Model and Constructivist Learning Theory informed the guide’s design logic, shaping elements that support perceived usefulness, ease of use, ethical decision-making, critical evaluation, and active engagement with learning. Rather than evaluating learning outcomes or performance gains, the article focuses on the development and rationale of a student-centred guidance artefact that complements institutional academic integrity policies. The resulting guide offers accessible and actionable support for students navigating ethical boundaries of GenAI use, while positioning AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for independent thinking or academic responsibility. Finally, it contributes a practice-oriented resource to ongoing discussions on academic integrity, student agency, and responsible GenAI use in AI-enabled higher education.

items.title: EAST: Embodied AI Safety Testing via Systematic Fault Injection in Digital Twins
items.abstract: Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. Existing evaluations often emphasize performance and robustness, but lack a systematic route from documented safety hazards to executable, verifiable tests. We present EAST (Embodied AI Safety Testing), a digital-twin framework that converts literature-grounded safety evidence into fault-injection tests across perception, instructions, environments, actions, and timing. EAST combines an expert-reviewed safety-fault taxonomy and eight executable operators with applicability and validity constraints. Its three-stage workflow generates test specifications, verifies fault realization during simulated execution, and independently assesses safety challenges, violations, task outcomes, and behavioral signatures using simulator-state evidence. The framework preserves execution traces and replayable records, supporting attribution and reproducibility across experiments. We evaluate EAST on six RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two policy architectures, ACT and RDT, against alternative testing strategies under matched budgets. Across five comparative campaigns, EAST targets all 74 admissible task-policy-operator combinations and obtains valid evidence for 63, while achieving safety-challenge exposure rates close to Random-Legal and Rule-Based. Moreover, 82 valid EAST executions complete their tasks despite safety violations, revealing risks concealed by success-oriented evaluation. These findings support systematic, validity-aware, reproducible safety testing beyond task-completion metrics.

items.title: Educational AI at the boundary of high risk: Estonia’s AI Leap as a stress test for the EU AI Act and the GDPR
items.abstract: Abstract Educational artificial intelligence (AI) does not become high-risk under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act 2024 merely because it is used in schools. Its classification depends on the function it performs within the educational process: whether it supports learning formatively, or whether it evaluates learning outcomes in ways that affect a student’s educational trajectory. This distinction is especially unstable in adaptive generative AI systems, where the same interactional features that make a tool pedagogically useful may, if repurposed or institutionally relied upon, move it towards the assessment logic of Annex III, point 3(b) of the AI Act. This paper uses Estonia’s AI Leap initiative as an early test case for that boundary. It develops four claims. First, the boundary between formative tutoring and high-risk assessment is conditional and dynamic, rather than inherent in the technology itself. Second, the profiling rule in Article 6(3) of the AI Act is best understood as an anti-derogation trigger: it does not independently bring a system within Annex III, but once an educational AI system falls within Annex III, profiling prevents reliance on the derogation from high-risk classification. Third, the initiative exposes a value-chain asymmetry characteristic of public-sector educational deployments built on third-party general-purpose AI models, in which downstream actors may acquire compliance responsibilities without full technical control. Fourth, Section 20¹ amendment to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act (Estonia) 2010 provides an unusually concrete national-law basis for educational AI processing, but it cannot by itself resolve the data-protection problems created by open-input generative systems, especially the incidental capture of special-category and third-party data. The paper concludes that the initiative’s regulatory significance lies less in its present classification than in the governance conditions needed to prevent functional drift and mitigate the data-protection risks created by open-ended student inputs.

items.title: EnerVision AI driven digital twin for predictive energy intelligence and sustainable manufacturing
items.abstract: Small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises form the backbone of industrial economies worldwide, yet they consistently struggle to monitor energy use, control energy cost, and meet sustainability targets because affordable, integrated decision-support tools remain scarce. This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven digital twin for energy optimization that unifies, within a single low-cost platform, five capabilities that prior studies address only in isolation: interpretable regression of energy against production, ensemble and recurrent Machine Learning (ML) models benchmarked for demand prediction and forecasting, generator-activation alerting, statistical anomaly detection, and a what-if scenario simulator with a decision-support dashboard. The framework ingests daily production volume together with grid-supplied and diesel-generator energy from an operating facility and derives Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for energy efficiency, Energy Per Unit of production (EPU), operating cost, and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. Linear and quadratic regression models link production to energy demand and are scored with the coefficient of determination (R2) and Root-Mean-Square error (RMSE); a Random Forest (RF) regressor, an exploratory RF generator-activation alert, and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for next-day forecasting are benchmarked against these interpretable baselines; because only six of the 59 valid daily observations were generator-active, the RF alert is not treated as a validated classifier. The principal novelty lies in integrating these complementary methods within one vendor-neutral digital twin aimed at resource-constrained enterprises. On a real case-study dataset, quadratic regression captures the production–energy relationship more closely than the linear baseline, and a load-shifting recommendation avoids generator use on the peak-demand day, reducing both cost and CO 2 emissions, while a 50% reduction in generator reliance yields substantial additional savings. A cross-validation study further shows that, in this small-data regime, higher-capacity ensemble and recurrent models do not improve out-of-sample accuracy over interpretable regression—an instructive finding that motivates the framework’s emphasis on transparent, deployable models for resource-constrained enterprises.

items.title: Enhancing Year 5 ESL Pupils’ Intrinsic Motivation through Google Classroom-Supported ESL Lessons: An Action Research Study
items.abstract: This study examined the use of Google Classroom-supported ESL lessons to enhance Year 5 pupils’ intrinsic motivation in learning English at a primary school in Pendang, Kedah. The study was conducted in response to concerns about pupils’ limited motivation and participation in English lessons, as well as the need for more structured use of digital learning platforms in primary ESL classrooms. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the study focused on three dimensions of intrinsic motivation: interest and enjoyment, perceived competence, and pressure and tension. An action research design was employed with 30 Year 5 ESL pupils. Over four weeks, the pupils participated in Google Classroom-supported ESL lessons that included structured vocabulary tasks, interactive activities, and teacher feedback. Data were collected using selected subscales from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory before and after the intervention. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The findings showed a statistically significant but modest change in pupils’ intrinsic motivation after the intervention. These findings suggest that Google Classroom may support pupils’ motivation when it is used as part of guided, interactive, and teacher-supported ESL lessons rather than as a stand-alone digital platform. The study contributes classroom-based evidence on the use of Google Classroom in Malaysian primary ESL education and highlights the importance of structured digital activities in supporting pupils’ motivation to learn English.

items.title: Evaluating Source-Grounded AI Technical Assistants for Higher Education: Technical Accuracy, Knowledge Boundaries, and Repeatability in Printing Technology
items.abstract: Source-grounded generative AI assistants can improve access to disciplinary literature, but citations do not ensure technical correctness. We evaluated two textile- and offset-printing assistants in Google NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), using 20 controlled prompts per assistant. One subject-matter expert rated technical accuracy, completeness, source support, and contextualization and manually checked citations. Mean overall scores were 4.73/5 and 4.61/5, respectively; because prompt sets differed, these are descriptive, not comparative. Source support exceeded technical accuracy in 35 of 40 original responses. In eight explicitly prompted knowledge-boundary tests, six responses showed appropriate abstention and two showed abstention with reservations; this evaluates prompted handling, not spontaneous recognition. Of seven repeated pairs with preserved identical wording, six received unchanged overall scores (mean absolute difference, 0.036/5); content comparison found recurring errors and differences across the ten pairs, although three offset pairs were only same-topic comparisons. A recurring textile error labeled source-reported heat-setting temperatures as glass-transition temperatures; a reported fabric-temperature rise applies only to vat-dye all-in cotton printing in saturated steam. With one expert evaluator and 15 original offset prompts preserved only as topic labels, this is an exploratory case study, not a validated benchmark. Student learning outcomes were not assessed.

items.title: Explainable AI for Intelligent and Sustainable Decision-Making
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve strategic planning, operational efficiency, and sustainability. However, conventional machine learning models often lack transparency, limiting managerial trust, accountability, and the practical adoption of AI-driven decisions. This study proposes an explainable AI (XAI) framework that integrates predictive analytics, interpretable machine learning, and sustainability indicators to support transparent, reliable, and evidence-based decision-making across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions. The proposed framework combines Random Forest, XGBoost, and Explainable Boosting Machines with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). Evaluation uses a benchmark dataset containing operational performance, resource consumption, organizational efficiency, and environmental indicators. Comparative experiments assess predictive accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), explanation consistency, decision latency, computational cost, and sustainability performance. Baseline models include Logistic Regression, conventional Random Forest, and XGBoost without explanation mechanisms. Ablation studies examine the individual contributions of interpretability and sustainability-aware optimization. The experimental evaluation is designed to determine whether the proposed framework improves predictive reliability, explanation quality, and sustainability-aware decisions compared with conventional approaches. Quantitative reporting will include percentage improvements in predictive performance, reductions in decision latency and resource consumption, and explanation stability across repeated experiments. Qualitative analysis will assess managerial understandability, perceived trustworthiness, fairness, and practical implementation challenges. Numerical outcomes will be reported only after experiments are completed, avoiding unsupported performance claims. The proposed framework establishes a comparative approach for integrating explainability, predictive intelligence, and sustainability into organizational decision-making. By connecting model predictions with transparent explanations and measurable sustainability indicators, the framework aims to strengthen accountability, operational effectiveness, and responsible technology adoption. Future validation across multiple industries will establish its generalizability and practical value. Keywords: Predictive Analytics; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Sustainable Decision-Making; Interpretable Machine Learning; Organizational Intelligence.

items.title: Fair AI in public administration: Estonia and EU law
items.abstract: Abstract This article examines fair and trustworthy artificial intelligence in public administration, presenting Estonia as the main case and EU law as the wider legal frame. It builds on the EquiTech project, which has been successfully co-implemented by the TalTech Department of Law and its project partners. The project materials, including training materials for public servants and data scientists, the project proposal, and related academic work, form an important empirical and normative basis for the article. The central claim is that fairness in public-sector artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be reduced to technical accuracy, general transparency, or compliance with a single legal instrument. Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell’s work on why fairness cannot be automated is the paper’s main theoretical anchor. Their concept of contextual equality helps explain why EU non-discrimination law does not translate easily into fixed fairness metrics, even though statistical evidence remains necessary. In the Estonian setting, this problem is visible in the gap between an advanced digital state and a still developing framework for assessing bias and discrimination risks across the full lifecycle of automated decision-making. The article argues that trustworthy public-sector AI requires legal authority, data governance, bias assessment, meaningful human oversight, administrative contestability, and institutional capacity. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is a major step in this direction, but it cannot by itself solve the legal and practical problems raised by algorithmic discrimination in public administration.

items.title: From Human Intent to In-Orbit Action: A Self-Learning Large Language Model Agent for 6G Satellite Networks
items.abstract: Autonomous control of sixth-generation (6G) low Earth orbit satellite networks is hindered by the gap between high-level human intent and low-level control logic: translating a request such as "uninterrupted Arctic video" into a valid reinforcement learning reward still takes days of manual trial and error, and existing large language model translators cannot learn from the failures of the policies they generate. This article presents ALMOND (Agentic Large-Model-Orchestrated autonomous Network Design), a cognitive framework that closes this intent-to-action loop under on-orbit compute constraints. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a bidirectional semantic engine that translates natural-language demands into multi-objective reward functions and, conversely, mines implicit operational constraints from failed reinforcement-learning trajectories through counterfactually validated forensics, together with a large language model-guided graph neuroevolution that seeds and critiques policy architectures. The contribution in engineering is a ground-centric, compute-frugal architecture for autonomous 6G non-terrestrial network operation, in which satellites execute only distilled policies below 50,000 parameters with sub-15 ms inference and no on-board large language model. On a 350-satellite digital twin driven by real ephemeris data, ALMOND raises polar handover success from 55% to over 95%, converges about three times faster than baseline reinforcement learning, and reduces reward engineering from 48 hours to 4.5 hours, demonstrating a practical path toward trustworthy in-orbit autonomy.

items.abstract: Since the release of diverse generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini,DALL-E, and GitHub Copilot, there has been much debate around the impacts and implications of thesetools on education. Currently, extant literature remarks on the affordances, challenges, and opportunitiesof GenAI, but few studies report and analyze empirical studies and educational practices coming up byGenAI usage in learning settings. Then, in this Scoping Review (ScR) based on 146 studies retrievedfrom the databases SCOPUS, Web of Science (WoS), and ERIC, we analyzed the implications ofintegrating GenAI in engineering and computing education from K-12 to tertiary levels. We adopted anapproach starting from the bibliometric features of the studies in terms of authors, cites, years, or clustertopics, and navigating to the identification of methodologies, strategies, AI literacy instruments andguidelines, learning outcomes, and students’ and teachers’ perceptions, among other features. Weadvocate that current educational practices in engineering and computing with GenAI can indicate to us aroadmap of its potentialities, uses, and risks from the standpoint of both teachers and students, and thiscould help us to create more reflexive methodologies that enhance the teaching-learning process based onthe evidence. Our purpose with the outcomes and conclusions of this scoping review is to supporteducators, faculty members, and other stakeholders in engineering and computing education to co-createeducational methodologies that articulate GenAI with curricula, AI literacy, and prompt engineeringencompassing students’ learning domains such as cognitive, affective, or behavioral. items.title: Honesty Testing of LLMs and AI Agents: A Vision for Software Engineering
items.abstract: Human oversight of large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) agents increasingly depends on their reports. Claims that conflict with a system's own judgments can conceal failures, prevent timely intervention, and contribute to severe harm. Greater autonomy makes faithful reporting increasingly important for maintaining human control. In this vision paper, we propose honesty testing of LLMs and AI agents as a new research area in software engineering. Building on existing honesty evaluations, our goal is to make faithful reporting a software quality requirement that developers can specify, test, and maintain. We define honesty bugs as behavioural defects in which an LLM or AI agent, when required to communicate faithfully, makes an explicit claim that conflicts with its own judgment at the time of reporting. We present an initial framework covering LLM-level testing under controlled inputs and agent-level testing of complete systems. The framework connects these levels to testing workflows and oracle evidence. We identify research directions in benchmarks, model and harness analysis, oracle construction, and lifecycle testing to support effective oversight alongside task correctness.

items.title: How Humans Learn Unfamiliar Worlds: A Think-Aloud Dataset on ARC-AGI-3
items.abstract: Learning through exploration and using newly acquired knowledge to achieve goals are central capabilities of general intelligence. Understanding these capabilities requires tracing how learners build, use, and revise world models during interaction. We construct the first dataset that records how humans discover and use the mechanisms of novel environments, using ARC-AGI-3 as a testbed: 144 trajectories from 64 participants across 25 public games, each pairing time-synchronized actions with think-aloud audio, plus 250 trajectories from large language model (LLM) agents with and without harnesses on the same games. We annotate mechanism triggers and recognition, action purposes, and errors and recovery, linking changes in understanding to the observations and actions that support them. We analyze characteristics of human cognition and compare them with those of LLM agents. Both groups anticipate mechanisms and use familiar analogies. Qualitative representations are more common in successful human trajectories than in successful LLM trajectories (50.0% versus 14.3%). Humans more often explore unfamiliar situations without a concrete hypothesis, while hypothesis testing is common in both groups. We also trace how learners recover through belief revision, replanning, and execution correction. As LLMs with well-designed harnesses reach saturated performance on public ARC-AGI-3 games, our cognitive analyses motivate next-generation benchmarks that challenge familiar priors, require accumulated evidence and abstraction, and test planning through subgoals, experimentation, and recovery. Our dataset is available at [https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/](https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/).

items.title: Human-in-the-Loop Intelligent Automation: A Review of Trust, Oversight, and Workforce Implications
items.abstract: Intelligent automation is now used to retrieve information, predict, recommend, generate content, route workflows and take physical or administrative action. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) design is often suggested as a possible fail-safe but it does not necessarily mean that a person is always in control. Oversight can be undermined by lack of time, authority, competence, independent evidence, or feedback or by a lack of real accountability despite the title of oversight. In this paper we explore HITL intelligent automation from three intertwined perspectives: calibrated trust, operational oversight, and workforce implications. It combines existing human-automation research, guidance for human–AI interaction, risk-management standards, regulation, and evidence of labor. A threat model encompasses technical misfortune, adversarial manipulation, cognitive and organizational failure, and harmful deployment of workforce. The mathematical formulation determines the automation modes based on expected error consequence, uncertainty, review cost, workload and skill preservation. The suggested architecture is that of separating the execution of the model from the risk routing, human decision making, dual authorization, audit, appeal, and learning feedback. A seeded synthetic experiment with 10,000 binary decisions is conducted for the comparisons between automation-only, passive universal review, risk-adaptive HITL, and dual control. With the declared generator, adaptive review achieves a 83.6% to 85.0% accuracy rate, while reviewing 37.1% of cases, and dual control achieves a 87.0% accuracy rate with a 5.2% rate of high impact error. These are indicative values and not measurements taken in the workplace. The review finds that effective HITL systems must have meaningful intervention capability, calibrated reliance, representative evaluation, protected worker voice, continuous competence and evidence of oversight functioning under realistic workload and failure.

items.title: HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION IN USER EXPERIENCE DESIGN: DEVELOPING AND VALIDATING A FRAMEWORK FOR AI-ASSISTED UI DESIGN
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, has transformed User Experience (UX) and User Interface (UI) design.Traditionally a human-centered discipline built on creativity, empathy, and iterative evaluation, UX design now increasingly involves AI tools that generate interface concepts, recommend components, analyse user behaviour, and support prototyping.Yet limited research examines how UX professionals actually collaborate with AI and what determines successful AI-assisted design practice.This research develops and validates a Human-AI Assisted UI Design Framework (HAUIDF), integrating Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HCAI), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Human-AI Teaming Theory, and Distributed Cognition Theory.The framework links AI transparency, explainability, and design capability; perceived usefulness, ease of use, and human control; AI trust and collaborative creativity; to UX productivity, design quality, designer satisfaction, and continued AI adoption intention.A mixed-method design is proposed: a quantitative survey of 300-400 UX professionals analysed with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4), complemented by 15-25 semi-structured interviews analysed thematically.The expected contribution is an empirically grounded account of AI as a collaborative design partner rather than an automation tool, offering theoretical contributions to HCI and AI-adoption research and practical guidance for designers, organizations, and AI tool developers pursuing human-centered AI workflows.

items.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
items.abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

items.title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila
items.abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

items.title: ISCR-SocioValidate: Reproducible Analysis Package for the Sociological Validation of the Integrated State Cyber Resilience (ISCR) Model
items.abstract: ISCR-SocioValidate is a Python package with documentation that makes the sociological validation of the Integrated State Cyber Resilience (ISCR) model reproducible. The ISCR model is a seven-layer governance architecture for state cyber resilience under hybrid threats. Its layers are strategic, institutional, operational-coordination, technological, human, legal, and international. The sociological validation asks whether professionals from cybersecurity-relevant sectors accept the model's proposals and which social and organizational preconditions they associate with its implementation. Version 0.1.0 works from a single file of published aggregate survey results (187 of 245 invited professionals) and recomputes every derived statistic and figure of the associated article: 95% Wilson score intervals for top-two-box agreement; an audit of the integer counts consistent with rounded percentages; reliability diagnostics (Cronbach's alpha, Spearman–Brown split-half reliability, implied mean inter-item correlation); a joint display that integrates closed-ended and open-ended evidence across the seven layers, using triangulation categories (agreement, partial agreement, silence, dissonance). Functions for intercoder agreement (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha) and item-level diagnostics prepare a respondent-level mode, which is under development. The record contains the source code, 13 unit tests, the aggregate input file with references to its source tables, a codebook template, generated tables (CSV), and Figures 1–2 (TIFF 800 dpi and PDF). It also includes documentation on the architecture, data schema, an analysis plan aligned with the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards, ethics and data governance, reproducibility, and a roadmap. No respondent-level or personal data are included, and no generative AI is used to code or interpret participants' answers. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later, numpy, pandas, matplotlib. items.title: K-12 AI literacy frameworks after generative AI: A scoping review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become a priority in K-12 education, yet frameworks for teaching and assessing it remain fragmented across grade levels, national contexts, and disciplinary traditions. This scoping review maps and synthesizes framework-level contributions to K-12 AI literacy published between January 2024 and December 2025. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, we searched four databases and grey literature sources, screened 204 unique records, and applied a purpose-built checklist covering five criteria: grade bands, competencies, critical constructs, assessment, and exemplars. Fifty studies met the inclusion threshold. The corpus spans 15 countries, with the United States (32%), Hong Kong (26%), and mainland China (12%) accounting for 70% of included studies. Frameworks defined AI literacy through cognitive, affective, behavioral, ethical, and social dimensions, but dimensional models used inconsistent labels and constructs, with limited crosswalk among them. The ABCE framework offered the closest approximation to a shared measurement tradition, with adaptation across three educational systems. Assessment and curriculum also developed largely in parallel: scale-development papers reported psychometric evidence without instructional sensitivity data, while curriculum papers assessed learning through lesson-linked tools that limited cross-study comparison. Generative AI competencies, including output evaluation, hallucination detection, and prompt design, remained peripheral in most frameworks despite their relevance to students’ everyday encounters with AI. Geographic concentration and limited attention to socioeconomic status, disability, and linguistic diversity further constrained transferability. The field needs stronger convergence through shared vocabulary, curriculum-aligned assessment, longitudinal evidence, and cross-context validation.

items.title: Learning by Collaborating in the Age of AI: Research Mentorship for Polymathic, Workflow-Centered Science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how data-driven research is produced. As AI tools make information and technical execution more accessible, mentorship must concentrate on judgment, ethics, and the design of end-to-end AI-augmented workflows. Disciplinary experts need mentoring to adopt AI while preserving their expertise and human agency, and AI-native research trainees need mentoring to become polymathic workflow developers. This chapter proposes Everyone's Backyard, an interdisciplinary model in which disciplinary experts, trainees, and community partners mentor one another in both directions and across disciplines through shared research practice in a convergence studio. The model centers on four capacities: statistical thinking, data ethics, collaboration, and AI for social good and society. We illustrate the model with the Spring 2026 aiX Faculty Fellows Program at Columbia University, which brought together 20 faculty fellows and 15 student interns from 14 schools and departments. Evaluation data show growth in faculty confidence, intern competence, and cross-disciplinary connection.

items.title: Machine Behavior: Paradigm Shift of Communication Research in AI Era
items.abstract: The widespread integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–driven communication agents, particularly large language models, has brought about a paradigm shift in communication research. Traditional human-centered paradigms are becoming inadequate for analyzing the behaviors and impacts of these non-human agents, which exhibit autonomous and intelligent communicative capabilities. This article advocates for the development of a Machine Behavior Paradigm in communication studies. This proposed paradigm explicitly expands the disciplinary scope by integrating machine behavior into three core dimensions. About research objects, it emphasizes the shifts from a human-only focus to a dual focus on humans and intelligent machines as communicative subjects. For research approaches, it should expand beyond human–human relationships to encompass machine–machine and hybrid human–machine interactions. In methodologies, we advocate to integrate computational indicators, such as text-generation temperature and activity frequency, alongside traditional empirical tools to address the opacity of AI “black boxes.” Furthermore, the article examines the limitations of current communication theories, such as agenda-setting and the spiral of silence, when applied to AI-driven environments. Also, we argue that it is difficult to study opaque AI systems with traditional methodologies. This shift necessitates interdisciplinary collaboration and the establishment of robust ethical guidelines to ensure the responsible study of autonomous agents. By outlining a systematic framework for individual, collective, and hybrid machine behavior, this article provides a roadmap for future inquiry.

items.title: ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?
items.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.

items.title: Reframing GenAI-mediated EFL speaking: A systematic review of empirical studies through an Activity Theory lens
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created more possibilities for English as a foreign language education. Through its generative capabilities, particularly in natural language generation and processing, GenAI has introduced new modes of interaction for learners’ speaking development. However, empirical research on GenAI-mediated EFL speaking remains fragmented. Guided by PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 43 empirical studies published between 2024 and 2026 to examine the trends, application methods, and challenges of GenAI-mediated EFL speaking activities. Findings indicate that research has focused primarily on mainland China and intermediate-level undergraduate learners, with ChatGPT as the most frequently used tool. GenAI was commonly used to provide personalized practice and immediate feedback in a comparatively low-pressure environment. Most studies reported positive outcomes, but findings varied. Behavioral outcomes received less attention than cognitive and affective aspects. Challenges mainly involved inauthentic interaction and limited feedback. Tensions are mainly from tools and subjects, as well as tools and objects from an Activity Theory lens. Based on these tensions, this study proposes a collaborative learning framework to provide complementary mediation in EFL speaking activities.

items.title: Responsible GenAI Augmentation and Cognitive Agency in Higher Education
items.abstract: Responsible generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) integration in higher education requires attention to useful assistance and students’ continuing cognitive agency. We examined how learner capability, cognitive offloading and institutional support relate to intention to use a university GenAI learning service, alongside reported reduced independent thinking. A cross-sectional survey of 593 students at one Thai public university was analyzed using ordinal structural equation modeling with WLSMV estimation. AI self-efficacy was positively associated with information utilization, utilization with perceived work efficiency, and efficiency with service intention. The serial indirect association was positive, while adjusted direct self-efficacy associations with efficiency and intention were inconclusive. Offloading was positively associated with both efficiency and reduced independent thinking. Its positive indirect association with intention through efficiency coexisted with a negative adjusted direct association. Institutional support was positively associated with intention. The prespecified TRUST comparison and additional covariates, screening and complete-case checks, retained the main association pattern. However, replacing utilization with information analysis reduced the analogous serial association, and reversing the utilization–efficiency link gave better descriptive fit. The findings therefore concern concurrent perceptions and reported practices, without establishing serial ordering or causal mediation. Independent learning and actual service engagement remain essential criteria for assessing educational value.
